# Supporting evidence for the Vignettes

**On fungal partners shared by eucalypt and elm trees:** English Elm (*Ulmus procera*) associates with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. Eucalypts associate with both arbuscular and ectomycorrhizal fungi, an adaptation to Australia's nutrient-poor soils [@tedersoo_distribution_2017]. Arbuscular associations are the more generalised of the two, are also used by many introduced trees including elms, and support young eucalypt roots. Ectomycorrhizal associations are more specialised, become more important as eucalypts mature, and supply mineral nutrients, water, and defence against pathogens [@tedersoo_distribution_2017]. A young Yellow Box growing among elms can therefore join arbuscular fungi that the elms already sustain, but it cannot obtain from them the ectomycorrhizal partners it will need as an adult. Eucalypts introduced outside Australia likewise form ectomycorrhizal partnerships with local fungi [@vlk_alien_2020].

**On the gardening of Mistletoebirds:** Ethological studies describe how Mistletoebirds (*Dicaeum hirundinaceum*) ‘garden’ mistletoe by depositing seeds near existing food patches. They can move as many as 66,000 mistletoe seeds per hectare in a season. Most seeds are wiped onto branches within already infected stands, reinforcing nearby food patches. Seventy per cent fall within 100 m of their source, 3 per cent travel beyond 500 m, and fewer than 5 per cent reach uninfected sites [@wardPredictingMistletoeSeed2007; @rawsthorneRestrictedSeedRain2012; @watsonMistletoeSpecialistFrugivores2013; @lowWhereSongBegan2014].

**On Mistletoebirds near the Parade place:** A 40-year study of Birrarung Park, a 33 ha reserve on the Yarra floodplain 17 km north-east of the Melbourne central business district and roughly 15 km east of the Parade place, recorded Mistletoebirds in 53 of 805 surveys, in 23 of the 40 years [@connorLongtermChanges402026]. Across metropolitan Melbourne the species is nomadic or irregular, and is recorded most often in outer-eastern riparian areas [@conoleFunctionalSpatialDifferentiation2011].

**On the mental maps of Blue-tongued Lizards:** Blue-tongued Lizards navigate using scent cues, which they use to build a mental map of where they have encountered females. In suburban Sydney, tracked Blue-tongued Lizards used drainage pipes, backyard sheds, concrete crevices, metal or timber piles, and other hard-cover shelters [@gravesDiscriminationSelfConspecific1991; @koenigEcologyAustralianReptile2001].

**On Eastern Blue-tongued Lizards at Royal Park:** The City of Melbourne's Nature in the City framework represents reptiles through the Eastern Blue-tongued Lizard (*Tiliqua scincoides*) and defines their habitat as mid-storey cover, understorey vegetation, and turf, with roads wider than five metres and all buildings acting as barriers [@kirk2018LinkingNatureIn]. The framework classes the whole of Royal Park as suitable reptile habitat,  yet finds reptiles the second least connected of its seven animal groups after amphibians, because roads, train lines, and tram lines fragment the park.

**On the lifespans of trees:** In cool European woodland, the closest wild comparator for English Elm (*Ulmus procera*), the *U. minor* lineage, can live for up to 400 years [cite]. In Melbourne, the oldest elms in Australia, at the Royal Botanic Gardens, are about 170 years old, roughly 50 years older than the oldest elms at the Parade place. Radiocarbon estimates place Yellow Box (*Eucalyptus melliodora*) lifespans at more than 700 years [@banksTreeAgesAgeing1997], while River Red Gums can live beyond a thousand years. Standing dead trees keep providing hollows, perches, bark, and ground refuge for decades after death [@le2014TheFutureOf]. Australian eucalypt wood on the ground takes from 7 years in *E. regnans* to 375 years in *E. camaldulensis* and *E. tereticornis* to decompose [@woldendorp2005CoarseWoodyDebris].

**On the importance of fallen wood:** Decayed wood left in place for longer periods releases different nutrients into soils by increasing the diversity of decomposer communities, because time raises the probability that mycelia or spores, including those of specialist and rare taxa with relatively poor dispersal abilities, will encounter woody material [@mallenCooper2026PlantAndSoilFunction].

**On the feasibility of Lace Monitors re-entering Melbourne:** Lace Monitors are now very rare in Melbourne, with occasional Green Wedge sightings [Manningham Council](https://www.manningham.vic.gov.au/climate-and-environment/living-natural-environment/manninghams-backyard-diversity-series). They are semi-arboreal and regularly climb trees for movement, refuge, and escape [Museums Victoria](https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8384); [Jones and Metcalfe 2013](https://varanidae.org/Vol7_No2.pdf). A 1.2 m adult climbed a 3 m external brick wall before a storm [Jones and Metcalfe 2013](https://varanidae.org/Vol7_No2.pdf), and Lace Monitors shelter in mature tree hollows.
